pamphlet_excerpts: Recognizing Fly-Fishing Perils: Even a gentle sport like fly-fishing can come with its perils (p. 77).
Essential Angler First Aid: A good angler will be well-versed in first-aid for cuts, scratches, puncture wounds, and insect bites and stings (p. 77).
Infection Risks From Wounds: Cuts and scratches are wounds, openings in the skin and tissues that can allow germs to enter the body and cause infection (p. 77).
Cleaning Minor Skin Cuts: Wash minor scratches and cuts with soap and water (p. 77).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Assess Open Skin Wounds: Cuts and scratches are wounds, openings in the skin and tissues that can allow germs to enter the body and cause infection (p. 77).
Step 2 - Wash Cuts With Soap: Wash minor scratches and cuts with soap and water (p. 77).
Step 3 - Clean and Rebandage Daily: On camping trips, clean and rebandage small wounds daily (p. 77).
Step 4 - Apply Direct Pressure First: Larger cuts should be treated with direct pressure to stop bleeding, then cleaned as well as possible to limit infection (p. 77).

pamphlet_excerpts: Matching Line and Rod: Lines vary by weight, and must be matched to the rod (p. 13).
Line Tapers and Buoyancy: They come in different styles (called tapers) and colors and are designed either to float on the surface of the water or to sink to different depths (p. 13).
Slow-Sinking Intermediate Fly Lines: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and can be fished just below the surface (p. 13).
Fast-Sinking Weighted Fly Lines: Heavily weighted lines sink quite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Intermediate Subsurface Line: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and can be fished just below the surface (p. 13).
Step 2 - Deploy Weighted Sinking Line: Heavily weighted lines sink quite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly (p. 13).
Step 3 - Practice With Floating Line: Most fly-fishing is done with floating lines, which are the easiest to cast and control (p. 13).
Step 4 - Target Deep Holding Fish: But there are times and conditions when fish lie deeply in the water and are not feeding at or near the surface (p. 13).

Step 3 - Tie Species-Specific Fly Patterns: The dry flies are tied in patterns to look like the specific species of insect (p. 38).
Step 4 - Match the Active Hatch: This is called matching the hatch, and itis one of the most important principles in fishing (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using Practice Casting Targets: A large plastic hoop (such as a hula hoop) makes an excellent target for practicing casting (p. 33).
Thumb-On-Top Cork Rod Grip: Make sure your thumb is on top of the rod's cork grip and that you have a firm hold (p. 33).
Stripping Out Working Line: Now, strip out 20 to 30 feet of line from the reel (p. 33).
Marking Thirty-Foot Casting Distance: You might want to make a mark 30 feet from the line tip, using a waterproof marker (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Strip Out Thirty Feet: Now, strip out 20 to 30 feet of line from the reel (p. 33).
Step 2 - Mark Line at Thirty: You might want to make a mark 30 feet from the line tip, using a waterproof marker (p. 33).
Step 3 - Lower the Rod Tip: With that length of line in front of you, more or less in a straight line, start with the rod tip down near the ground or the surface of the water (p. 33).
Step 4 - Accelerate and Stop Abruptly: Smoothly accelerate the rod through the vertical, or 12 o'clock, position and then stop it abruptly (p. 33).
